\newcommand{\EigenxCommit}{d89d790}
\newcommand{\MethodText}{%
One campaign, run \texttt{\BenchRunId}, measured every operation on one host: a
shared cloud VM with 4 vCPUs (Intel Xeon at 2.10\,GHz, one thread per core),
Linux 6.18, rustc~1.97.0, release profile, \art{eigenx} commit
\texttt{\EigenxCommit}. Isolation is the lowest level (L0): no core pinning
for the all-core rows, and \texttt{taskset -c 0} for the single-core rows.
Other tenants' load is not controlled. The harness is
\art{eigenx:examples/bench_kem.rs}.
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item For each set it draws several fresh keys. Key generation is timed in
  wall time and in process CPU time, because it is a rejection search: a
  single sample says little, and parallel attempts (\texttt{jobs}) trade
  CPU time for wall time.
\item Under each key it runs encapsulation then decapsulation of an honest
  ciphertext several times, one PKE round trip of a 1\,KiB message with
  associated data, and one public-key degree test, the attacker's oracle
  (\S\ref{sec:security}). Every result is checked.
\item In the same binary it times $\F_p$ and $\F_{p^2}$ arithmetic.
\end{itemize}
Samples per set: L1 5 keys $\times$ 10, L3 and L5 5 $\times$ 5, Q3 2
$\times$ 3, Q5 1 $\times$ 3, and single-core L1 2 $\times$ 5, L3 and L5 1
$\times$ 3. The Q sets use \texttt{jobs}=4 for key generation; every other
row uses \texttt{jobs}=1. Medians are reported with the range, because the
samples are few and the host is noisy.}
\newcommand{\PerfDiscussion}{%
\paragraph{Reading the numbers.}
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item \emph{Decapsulation dominates online cost.} It is a $(2^E,2^E)$
  theta chain plus pairings and a re-encryption. At L1 it is about six
  times the cost of encapsulation, a 3-isogeny chain of length $F$. Across
  sets it scales roughly as $E\cdot M(p)$, where $M(p)$ is the
  $\F_{p^2}$ multiplication time of Table~\ref{tab:field}.
\item \emph{Threads.} Decapsulation runs four independent ladders and the
  chain's two Montgomery conversions in parallel. On one core it is about
  1.6 times slower at L1 and 1.7 times at L3 and L5
  (Table~\ref{tab:onecore}). Encapsulation barely changes.
\item \emph{Key generation is a rejection search.} Its time per key varies
  by up to a factor of two within a set, so medians over five keys are
  rough. With \texttt{jobs}=4, Q3 used 2.4--2.8\,ks of CPU per key, finished
  in 11.5--15.7 minutes of wall time, and used the four cores at about 75\%.
  L5 key generation is faster than L3 at the median. The rejection rate,
  not the field size, sets the cost, and five samples cannot resolve the
  difference.
\item \emph{PKE} adds one ChaCha20-Poly1305 pass to the KEM. For a 1\,KiB
  message it is indistinguishable from the KEM times.
\item \emph{Comparison with the historical build.} Revision~1 of the
  companion paper measured decapsulation with a Mumford-coordinate chain:
  13.4--15.0\,s at L1, 51.8--53.9\,s at L3 and 120--124\,s at L5, on a
  2.80\,GHz VM. The theta build is roughly 10 times faster at every L set.
  Those are different hosts, so treat this as an order of magnitude, not a
  measured speedup.
\item \emph{No external comparison.} No other implementation of this
  scheme exists, so there is no external tool to compare against.
\end{itemize}}
